title: When Λ Breaks: How a Ten-Percent Departure from w = −1 Rewrites the Expansion History, the Age and the Ultimate Fate of the Universe
content: The ΛCDM model assumes that dark energy is a cosmological constant with equation-of-state parameter w = −1, yet recent baryon acoustic oscillation data have revived interest in dynamical dark energy. This study asks how the cosmic expansion rate changes when w departs from −1. We solve the Friedmann equation for a spatially flat universe containing radiation, matter and dark energy with constant w, comparing ΛCDM (w = −1), a quintessence-like case (w = −0.9) and a phantom case (w = −1.1), with H₀ = 67.4 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ and Ωm = 0.315 held fixed. We compute the Hubble parameter H(z), deceleration parameter q(z), acceleration-transition redshift, dark-energy fraction, cosmic age, luminosity distance and distance modulus. Relative to ΛCDM, the expansion rate is up to 2.6% higher for w = −0.9 (peak at z ≈ 0.69) and up to 2.3% lower for w = −1.1 (peak at z ≈ 0.61); the differences fade above z ≈ 3 as matter dominates. Present-day acceleration strengthens monotonically as w decreases (q₀ = −0.42, −0.53, −0.63), and the cosmic age shifts from 13.58 to 13.79 to 13.98 Gyr. Surprisingly, the deceleration–acceleration transition redshift barely moves (zt ≈ 0.62–0.63), whereas the matter–dark-energy equality epoch shifts from z = 0.33 to 0.27. Distance moduli differ by only ≈ 0.04 mag at z ≈ 1–1.5, at the edge of current supernova precision. The phantom case ends in a Big Rip about 116 Gyr from now. A ten-percent change in w therefore leaves a small but measurable fingerprint on the past and a radically different future.
